opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and one I think about a lot, partly because I don't think there's a single right answer. My instinct is that it should be pretty decentralized. Some of the most interesting work in NLP has come from people who were a little out of step with where the field was going at the time. If everyone converges on the same benchmark or the same scaling recipe, we lose the diversity of ideas that actually moves things forward.

That said, I don't think "let a thousand flowers bloom" is a complete answer either. There are real structural forces shaping what people work on: compute access, what gets accepted at conferences, what industry labs are hiring for, what's easy to publish quickly. Those forces aren't neutral, and a lot of the time they push people toward incremental work on whatever's popular. So part of making good decisions as a community is being honest about those incentives and trying to counterbalance them, for example by valuing careful empirical studies, negative results, and work that asks "why does this work?" rather than just "can I get another point on the leaderboard?"

I also think academia has a particular role to play right now. We're not going to out-scale the big labs, and we shouldn't try. But we can do things they're less incentivized to do: open, reproducible science, understanding and analysis, efficiency, and questions that don't have an obvious commercial payoff. Academics should pick directions where being small and curious is an advantage, not a liability.

And at the individual level, my advice to students is usually: work on something you find genuinely interesting and where you have some unusual angle. If you'd be one of a hundred groups doing the same thing, it's worth asking whether your contribution really matters. The field benefits when people take a few bets that look a bit weird at the time.

r002.rationale: It supports diversity and taking unusual bets, but does not clearly advocate an environment where people feel comfortable experimenting.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, partly because the field has gotten so big that nobody actually makes those decisions anymore. There's no central committee. The direction emerges from thousands of individual choices about what to work on, what to review favorably, what to fund, what to put on Twitter.

So I'd reframe it a bit. The question isn't really "who should decide," it's "what incentives are shaping the decisions people are already making," and whether those incentives are healthy.

Right now I'd say they're mixed. The good part is that there's a lot of fast, open iteration. Someone puts out an idea, and within weeks people have tested it, broken it, extended it. That's genuinely great, and it's something NLP does better than most fields.

The worrying part is how much gravitational pull the big labs have. If one well-resourced group releases a model and sets an agenda, a huge fraction of the academic community reorganizes around it, often around things like benchmark chasing or prompting tricks that are downstream of decisions made somewhere else. That's not because academics are unimaginative. It's because the tools they can afford are shaped by what's been released, and the reviewers expect you to compare against the thing everyone's talking about.

What I'd like to see is more deliberate diversification. Academics in particular should be asking "what can I do that a company structurally won't?" That might mean work on efficiency, on interpretability, on languages that aren't commercially interesting, on building open infrastructure that lets other people do research at all. It might mean being willing to work on something that looks unfashionable for a few years.

And I'd put some responsibility on the community institutions too. Conferences and reviewing have a lot of implicit power over direction. If reviewing rewards incremental state-of-the-art bumps on a leaderboard, you get a field that optimizes for that. If it rewards clarity, reproducibility, and genuinely new questions, you get something different. Those are choices, even if no one experiences them as choices.

So the short version is: decisions get made bottom-up whether we like it or not, and the lever we actually have is shaping the incentives and making sure the open, academic part of the field keeps asking its own questions rather than just reacting.

r002.rationale: It praises fast, open iteration and calls for diversification, but does not say people should feel comfortable experimenting to encourage new ideas.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss early deep-learning work lacking a clear home in machine learning or NLP.

astra-6.text:
I think it should be fairly decentralized. One of the things I like about research is that people can follow an intuition that other people don’t share. If we all agree on what the important problems are, we risk having everyone work on the same thing and missing something interesting.

But the incentives matter a lot. What gets published, what gets funded, what we recognize as a contribution—all of that influences which directions people feel they can pursue. So I’d want those processes to leave room for different kinds of work: building systems, understanding why something works, studying language, or finding a problem that our current benchmarks don’t capture.

And researchers shouldn’t be the only people in that conversation. If we’re building systems that people are going to use, we need to listen to those people about what’s useful and what’s going wrong. I don’t think that gives you a single roadmap for NLP, but it gives you a healthier way to choose what to work on.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly favors a decentralized approach and says researchers should be able to pursue intuitions others do not share.

r002.rationale: It advocates incentives and processes that leave room for different kinds of work, so researchers can follow unconventional ideas and uncover something interesting.

r003.rationale: The response does not connect its preference for decentralized research to any experience of failing to predict NLP’s direction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it should be a pretty decentralized process. One of the strengths of research is that people have different intuitions about what matters, and they can pursue those ideas without everybody agreeing on a single direction. I’d be wary of deciding, as a field, that there’s one problem or one approach we should all work on.

But the choices aren’t made in a vacuum. What gets funded, what gets accepted at conferences, and what resources people have access to all influence what researchers can do. So I think we need to be thoughtful about those incentives and make room for people to challenge the prevailing approach. Ideally, you want a field where a student with a compelling idea can try it, even if it isn’t what the largest labs are doing.
